narrative:
Your application was reviewed by a predictive model that assessed your likelihood of passing the bar exam on the first attempt, and the model estimated a 51% probability that you would not pass — a slim but decisive margin that resulted in your application being rejected. This means the decision was not clear-cut; you are very close to the threshold, and relatively modest improvements in your profile could shift the outcome in your favor.

To help you understand what would need to change, the model was tested against a series of "what if" scenarios — alternative versions of your profile where certain factors were adjusted just enough to flip the prediction from "likely to fail" to "likely to pass." These scenarios, called counterfactuals, don't reflect judgments about who you are, but rather highlight which levers, if pulled, would make the most difference in how the model evaluates your application.

Across 10 such alternative scenarios that were generated for your profile, one pattern emerged with striking consistency: your LSAT score was the only factor that changed in every single one of them. Your academic decile rankings, family income background, undergraduate GPA, and enrollment status remained unchanged across all 10 scenarios — meaning the model does not see those as the deciding factors in your case. This is a remarkably focused signal: the model is essentially telling you that your LSAT score is the single key to unlocking a different outcome.

Your current LSAT score of 34 sits below the average of approximately 37 among students who successfully passed the bar exam, and the counterfactual scenarios suggest that an average increase of just 2 points — bringing your score to around 36 — would be sufficient to tip the prediction in your favor. That is a meaningful but achievable gap. It's worth noting that in other respects, your profile has genuine strengths: your undergraduate GPA of 3.70 is actually well above the average of 3.24 among students who passed, which is a real asset that the model already recognizes and holds constant across all scenarios.

Your first- and third-year academic decile rankings of 3 and 1, respectively, are notably lower than the averages of around 6 seen among students who passed, and your part-time enrollment status is less common among successful bar passers — yet the model did not identify changes to these factors as necessary to flip your prediction. This suggests that while those factors contribute to the overall picture, your LSAT score is the most actionable lever available to you right now. Focusing your energy on LSAT preparation — through targeted practice, prep courses, or tutoring — and aiming for a score improvement of at least 2 points could realistically move your application from rejected to approved.
